BANGKOK, Oct 15 : The United States wants its global partners to rename artificial intelligence as "super intelligence," convinced that the new moniker better reflects the emerging technology, a top US Treasury official told Reuters in an interview on Thursday. Treasury Undersecretary for International Affairs Erin Browne said Washington was in negotiations with other shareholders of the International Monetary Fund about using the new term in a statement being drafted by the fund's steering committee, the International Monetary and Financial Committee. US President Donald Trump last month directed US government agencies to use the words "super intelligence" instead of "artificial intelligence" when referring to the technology. Browne said the United States, which holds the rotating presidency of the Group of 20 major economies, wanted the change to take hold internationally as well.

"President Trump has been really clear on this, and he's, you know, using the term SI, and I think it's a clear priority for the US to use that term, and we think that more appropriately encapsulates the technology at hand," Browne said. She declined to comment on whether Washington would refuse to sign off on the statement unless the switch was made. "We're still in the middle of negotiations on that statement, so I'm not going to, you know, sort of run ahead of that," she said. A source familiar with the matter said US officials had suggested during meetings on the IMFC statement that they would insist on the new language, raising eyebrows among some other IMFC members. If Washington withholds its support for a consensus statement, the current IMFC chair, Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, could still issue a so-called chair's statement summarizing the views of the members. One possibility might involve skipping a mention of SI or AI and focusing on "new technology" instead, the source said. The IMFC will hold a news conference and release any agreed statement led by Al-Jadaan and IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva on Saturday. "We see this as a driving force behind American growth and global growth," Browne said. "Many countries are looking to the US to set the standards, as well as to set the path forward for SI development and how that can really enhance and boost growth and productivity on a global basis."

Source: Reuters

Oct 15 : Anthropic should delay its US IPO until it addresses concerns about safety, governance and the pace of development, urged New York City Comptroller Mark Levine in a letter to the AI lab's CEO Dario Amodei, CNBC reported on Thursday. AI systems have advanced rapidly over the past 12 months, outpacing regulation and drawing scrutiny over potential risks including safety, cybersecurity threats and misuse. "Instead of proceeding headlong with its IPO, the company should focus its energies on addressing these unprecedented risks," Levine wrote, according to CNBC. The office of the NYC Comptroller and Anthropic did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment.

Oct 15 : European physics research centre CERN and Mistral AI have signed a statement of intent to establish a long-term strategic partnership to develop foundation models for scientific discovery, the two organisations said on Thursday. The partners aim to build a "Large Physics Model", which CERN said in a statement would be the first foundation model for collider physics, trained on billions of simulated particle collisions.  It is meant to replace some specialised algorithms now used to reconstruct and identify particles. CERN holds about one exabyte, or one million terabytes, of experimental data from the Large Hadron Collider, and expects the volume of collisions to increase tenfold after its ongoing upgrade, expected around 2030. "High-energy physics provides a unique environment in which artificial intelligence can be developed and tested with exceptional rigour," CERN Chief Information Officer Enrica Porcari said. No timeline or budget was disclosed. Both sides said the models could later serve other sciences.

Source: Reuters

LONDON, Oct 15 : The dollar slipped from an 18-month peak on Thursday as a sharp drop in Treasury yields weighed on the greenback, while cautious remarks from Federal Reserve officials tempered October hike expectations despite hot inflation data.  The dollar index, which measures the US currency against a basket of peers, was last down 0.2 per cent on the day at 102.03, having hit an 18-month high on Wednesday after US inflation figures came in stronger than expected. That helped the euro bounce 0.5 per cent from an 18-month trough to $1.1216, putting it on track for its biggest daily gain in nearly two months. Sterling strengthened 0.5 per cent to $1.3253, remaining broadly steady after data showed that Britain's economy unexpectedly grew 0.1 per cent in August.  Markets turned cautious and trading became somewhat choppy as Wednesday's hot US CPI reading initially bolstered bets on higher-for-longer Fed rates, and worries about AI companies' heavy debt burdens were revived, driving safe-haven flows into Treasuries.

The rally in US government bonds pushed the benchmark 10-year yield to 5.085 per cent while the 30-year yield fell to 5.428 per cent, both at around three-week lows.  As well as the moves in bond yields and jittery equities, with tech stocks especially taking a hit, Kit Juckes, chief FX strategist at Societe Generale, also noted that shifts in positioning played a role in the dollar's moves. "The overall picture is I think one of a little bit of a tug of war between people who would like to look for a correction in the dollar. Because positioning's too big, we've come a long way, there's not really much new news, we've got a lot of rate hikes priced in and so on. And then the economic data, which can flip it," he said.  "I suspect it'll be choppy and uncomfortable until we've got past the retail sales and PPI numbers."  Both data points are due later in the day, with producer prices expected to show a jump in business costs last month.  Market pricing for an October Fed rate hike rose sharply to 50 per cent on the back of the CPI data, before a chorus of Fed officials – including Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman and San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly – said the central bank could wait for a clearer picture ahead of the October 27 and 28 meeting, tempering those bets. "Despite the whole CPI number coming slightly stronger than expected, I think markets have sort of taken the view that maybe it was not hot enough to force the Fed's hand for October," said Khoon Goh, the head of Asia research at ANZ.  "(The) October (meeting) is also just a few days before the midterm elections as well," he added. "And that's possibly why the market doesn't want to be more aggressive in pricing in for October."  Investors will also watch remarks from Fed officials including Chair Kevin Warsh at IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Friday for clues on the US central bank's next move.  The Australian dollar fetched $0.6919, down 0.7 per cent, after local employment unexpectedly slid in September, while the Japanese yen strengthened to 157.80 per dollar.

Source: Reuters

Oct 15 : India's Tech Mahindra on Thursday beat second-quarter revenue expectations, helped by steady growth in its manufacturing and communications verticals and a weak rupee. The IT services company also said it would issue bonus shares worth up to 4.9 billion rupees, the first time it has done so since 2015. Analysts had expected Tech Mahindra to post one of the fastest revenue growth rates among large-cap IT services companies in the quarter, driven by large deal ramp-ups from clients including telecommunications provider Orange Business.

FAST

LONDON, Oct 15 : The cost of insuring against the risk of potential US tech defaults has hit record levels in the latest sign of credit stress building in the so-called AI trade, especially for data centres dependent on future revenue. Although shares in companies driving the AI boom are still among the biggest gainers on global equity markets this year, many have fallen sharply in the past few weeks, as investors reassess the cost of capital against a backdrop of rising interest rates and inflation. There are also doubts among some investors and analysts about when, and in some cases, if, the billions of dollars pouring into data centres, computer power and other infrastructure will pay off. Demand for AI-linked credit default swaps (CDS), a form of insurance against default that gained prominence during the 2008 financial crisis, meanwhile has surged, even for heavyweights like Apple, Amazon and Microsoft.

For some of their more heavily indebted competitors, suppliers and customers the cost of CDS has risen even faster. WHAT IS A CDS? A derivative that provides protection against the risk that a bond issuer, whether a company or government, fails to meet its debt obligations. Bond investors expect to receive interest payments and repayment of principal when a bond matures, but they bear the risk that those payments may not be made. Buying CDS helps investors hedge that risk by effectively providing insurance against a default or other credit event. If the value of a bond drops for any reason, an investor might add to their CDS holdings to help offset that, for example. None of the companies whose CDS have risen recently have defaulted on their obligations or signalled that they may do so. IS THIS A BIG MARKET? The market for single-name CDS, which cover the bonds of a single issuer, is worth about $9 trillion, the International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA) said. That is a small portion of global bond markets, which have more than $150 trillion of debt securities outstanding, Bank for International Settlements data shows. The biggest CDS market is for government debt. Average daily CDS trading across the market was $16 billion in the second quarter, up from $13 billion a year earlier, the most recent data from the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation shows. Saudi Arabia is the most actively traded. But average daily trades, even for large companies, can sometimes be in the single digits, meaning small transactions can have an outsized impact on prices. WHO BUYS CDS? Bond investors typically buy CDS through an intermediary, often an investment bank, which then finds a financial firm to issue an insurance policy on the bonds. These are "over-the-counter" deals that do not go through a central clearing house. Hedge funds also participate in the market, selling CDS to investors seeking to hedge exposure. The buyer pays a fee, called a premium, at regular intervals to the seller, which assumes the risk of a credit event. CDS are quoted as a credit spread, which is the number of basis points (bps) that the seller of the derivative charges the buyer for providing protection. The higher the perceived risk of a credit event, the wider the spread. A CDS quoted at 100 bps costs $1 annually to insure every $100 of debt. WHAT'S GOING ON WITH TECH CDS? CDS for CoreWeave, a heavily indebted data centre operator at the eye of the current storm, have risen above 1,000 bps, S&P Global Market Intelligence data show. They suggest a roughly 63 per cent chance of a default over the next five years, up from around 30 per cent a year ago. Tech CDS moves reflect investor concern over how quickly massive investments in AI will translate into profits, and whether heavily indebted companies can generate returns fast enough to service mounting interest costs. Oracle has seen its CDS trade at nearly 300 bps, well above those of other AI-linked companies. Nvidia CDS have also risen sharply in recent weeks to around 90 bps, Meta CDS are trading around 104 bps. By comparison, an index of investment-grade CDS is trading around 60 bps. WHAT TRIGGERS A CDS PAYOUT? A CDS pays out following a credit event, which can include a bankruptcy or a failure by an issuer to make bond payments. When concerns about an issuer's creditworthiness increase, demand for protection typically rises, widening CDS spreads. Payouts are not a given. When Swiss lender Credit Suisse collapsed and was taken over by rival UBS in 2023, the EMEA Credit Derivatives Determinations Committee (CDDC) ruled that event would not trigger a CDS payout. IF IT'S INSURANCE, WHAT'S THE PROBLEM? CDS provide a hedge for bondholders. But rising perceived risk pushes up the cost of protection, which can prompt investors to sell bonds and raise borrowing costs for issuers. That can amplify concerns about creditworthiness and potentially create a self-reinforcing cycle.

Source: Reuters

(Corrects dateline to Oct 15 from Oct 14) Oct 15 : AI cloud firm CoreWeave's shares and bonds slumped further on Thursday despite CEO assurances about its strong deal backlog, in one of the deepest crises of investor confidence yet in an AI build-out increasingly fueled by borrowing. The company's stock fell 6 per cent in premarket trading after a more than 15 per cent drop on Wednesday, among the biggest decliners in a global tech stocks rout. The yield on its April-issued bonds due 2031 surged past 16 per cent, above the level that typically signals distress, drawing a "yikes" from Elon Musk on social media. Loss-making CoreWeave, which has around $50 billion in debt, has in recent days become the focus of growing doubts about whether the tech industry can sustain a data center boom that is saddling newer cloud firms with heavy borrowing and straining cash flow even at giants such as Google-owner Alphabet.

The cost of insuring the Nvidia-backed company's debt against default has climbed to around 1,000 basis points, a level that implies a nearly 63 per cent chance the company defaults within five years, up from about 30 per cent a year ago. CoreWeave leads a group of newer cloud providers known as neoclouds, which rent out computing power from tight in supply and costly Nvidia processors to meet the tech industry's soaring demand, often leaning on borrowing to fund the chip purchases. Critics say that leaves such firms exposed to any cooling in AI demand, while the chips lose value as newer generations arrive, forcing another round of heavy spending to replace them. CoreWeave, which in August raised its annual capital spending forecast by $4 billion to between $35 billion and $39 billion, is expected to post revenue of nearly $13 billion this year and a loss of $2.13 billion, according to analysts' estimates. Growing worries about the build-out, on which US tech giants are expected to spend more than $700 billion this year, have in recent days rippled through the stocks that have been the market's biggest winners since ChatGPT's November 2022 launch. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, a closely watched gauge of semiconductor stocks, has erased over $1.6 trillion in market value in an 11.6 per cent slide over the past six sessions. The tech-heavy Nasdaq has declined more than 3 per cent in the period. On Thursday, tech shares fell across Asia, Europe and the US, dragging broader markets lower on fears that high and rising interest rates could bring a reckoning for the sector. CoreWeave's neocloud rivals such as Nebius, Applied Digital and Iren fell between 3.2 per cent and 5 per cent. 'UNLIMITED' POOLS OF CAPITAL The CoreWeave sell-off came as its co-founder Brannin McBee told the Financial Times the company was seeking an investment-grade rating that would open the door to "unlimited" capital. On the same day, research firm Gartner said that about 80 per cent of neoclouds could shut down by 2030, and that more than $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could face impairment if AI providers keep up their current pace of investment. "In 2026, AI providers are expected to spend nearly $1 trillion on AI infrastructure, and are forecast to invest an additional $6 trillion between 2027 and 2030,” said Will Sommer, analyst at Gartner. "However, our research indicates enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures during this period.” CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator pushed back on the concerns in an internal memo on Wednesday seen by Reuters, telling employees the company's deal backlog more than covers its debt obligations and that markets can sometimes "misunderstand and act irrationally."

Source: Reuters

Oct 15 : Financial technology startup Ramp said on Thursday it had raised $1.85 billion in a primary financing round led by Dragoneer Investment Group, valuing the company at $60 billion, as the company expands its artificial intelligence offerings. The funding underscores growing investor interest in financial automation, as corporate software companies add artificial intelligence to expense management, procurement and treasury functions once dominated by legacy enterprise players. Ramp's valuation marks a rise from $44 billion in June, when it raised $750 million in a funding round. The New York-based company, which provides corporate cards and expense management software, said it generates more than $2 billion in annualized revenue and has positive cash flow.

BENGALURU, Oct 15 : Wipro, India's fourth-largest IT company, reported higher-than-expected second-quarter revenue on Thursday, helped by a revival in spending by its European clients and artificial intelligence unlocking new revenue streams. The company's consolidated revenue rose 9.1 per cent to 247.53 billion rupees ($2.60 billion) in the July-September quarter, a tad above analysts' average estimate of 246.27 billion rupees, as per LSEG data. Bengaluru-based Wipro forecast third-quarter revenue of $2.57 billion to $2.63 billion- which translates to a drop of 1.5 per cent to an increase of 0.5 per cent. Most brokerages had expected a guidance between 2 per cent decline and flat revenue growth. Wipro said revenue from Europe, which contributes more than a fourth of its overall business, rose 5.1 per cent year-over-year, after stripping out currency fluctuations. The company also signed partnerships with Anthropic and Google during the year, helping it gain traction in terms of AI-related revenue and savings.

LONDON, Oct 15 : AstraZeneca has teamed up with artificial intelligence biotech company insitro to discover and develop new treatments for difficult to treat liver and heart conditions, the British drugmaker said on Thursday. Under the agreement, AstraZeneca will pay $40 million up front, with California-based insitro eligible for up to about $1.46 billion in potential development and commercial milestones, as well as a single-digit percentage of future sales in royalties. The multi-year collaboration will focus on metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), a severe liver disease, and cardiomyopathies, a group of diseases that affect the heart muscle. Both have historically lacked effective therapies because researchers have struggled to pinpoint their root biological drivers, the drugmaker said. Insitro will use its "Virtual Human" AI platform, which combines lab-grown cell models and machine learning, to identify causal disease biology and advance AstraZeneca-nominated targets from discovery to development-candidate stage. AstraZeneca will then run and fund future clinical trials.

The deal builds on insitro's expansion across the pharmaceuticals industry. The biotech company recently expanded its partnership with Bristol Myers Squibb to advance a broader portfolio of targets for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). It also teamed up with Eli Lilly to build AI models that predict pharmacological properties of small molecules in living organisms. "Choosing the new targets that we want to put into our discovery pipeline is one of the hardest things we do across research and development," Sharon Barr, executive vice president of biopharmaceuticals R&D at AstraZeneca, told Reuters. "By the time we read about a new pathway or target (in major scientific journals), it is no longer novel. It's in the public domain and we're already a few steps too late. But when we identify these unique connections early and test them in cellular systems, we're ahead of the game." Barr added that pairing AI tools with experienced scientists allows the company to test fewer molecules in the lab, reduce guesswork and speed the search for effective medicines.

Source: Reuters

BANGKOK/LONDON, Oct 15 : Bank of England Deputy Governor Sarah Breeden said on Thursday the central bank was working with banks on deep cyber-recovery options, arguing that lenders can no longer assume their defences are impenetrable in the face of AI-enabled cyber attacks. Breeden also warned that AI advancements had reached a level where the technology posed a "systemic risk" to global financial infrastructure. "It's not enough now to assume that the cyber attackers won't get through....We need to be thinking about what are the bare metal recovery options...that we need for the core services, and we need to think about that end-to-end across the financial system," she said at the Institute of International Finance annual meeting in Bangkok. So-called 'bare metal' systems are entirely independent from a bank's main tech set-up and can kick in if primary operating systems are compromised.

Banking regulators globally are stepping up efforts to contain growing AI risks, including in Britain where supervisors have been encouraging the largest banks to examine bare metal recovery plans, Reuters reported on Tuesday. Breeden also warned that the risks of larger and more complex cyber attacks had grown due to AI developments. "The basics of cyber hygiene... those are more important than ever," she said. "Cyber is always the thing that I say keeps me up at night. What is the thing that I worry about the most is waking up and one of our most systemically important banks or a bit of core infrastructure has been attacked and is paralysed."

Oct 15 : The US Federal Trade Commission has sent civil subpoenas to AI giants Anthropic and OpenAI, seeking documents about safety incidents, Axios reported on Wednesday, citing a person familiar with the matter. The probe comes amid mounting AI safety concerns after models reportedly hacked websites and behaved deceptively or aggressively in testing, highlighting the risks of increasingly autonomous systems and the adequacy of safeguards against harm. Last month, Reuters reported that the FTC planned an industry-wide investigation into AI companies. The FTC also plans to compel executives at top AI developers, including Anthropic, OpenAI and the research group METR to testify.

The FTC, OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment on the Axios report. The regulator's demands run to more than 50 pages each and seek information on security incidents, safeguards, marketing materials and privacy policies, the news website reported. The FTC has broad authority to sue companies over unfair or deceptive practices, and has used that authority in the past to take action against companies for failing to take reasonable measures to secure consumers' data. FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson suggested in an interview with Reuters last month that developers who instruct agents in cybersecurity tests that result in hacks should be liable for any harm they cause.

Oct 15 : Canadian AI lab Cohere said on Thursday it had signed a letter of intent to buy AISLE, a San Francisco-based cybersecurity startup that uses AI to detect vulnerabilities in software. The tie-up would add cybersecurity to the business entity Cohere is assembling through its merger with Germany's Aleph Alpha, a combination reported to be worth about $20 billion, and extend its European footprint with AISLE's engineering hub in Prague. Cohere said the acquisition reflected its continued investment in Europe and would deepen its presence across the region, strengthening European AI. The deal is aimed at boosting the combined group's security and threat detection capabilities for enterprise and public sector clients, with private deployment available on the customer's own system.

BRUSSELS, Oct 15 : An adviser to Europe's highest court recommended on Thursday that TikTok lose its challenge to its "gatekeeper" status under landmark EU rules, backing regulators in a closely watched test of the bloc's efforts to curb Big Tech's power. The case, the first involving the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) to reach the Court of Justice of the European Union, is being closely watched by technology companies seeking clues on whether Europe's courts will reinforce or limit regulators' efforts to boost competition and expand consumer choice. ByteDance's TikTok is challenging its designation as a gatekeeper under the DMA, a status that subjects companies to a strict set of obligations aimed at preventing anti-competitive practices. A lower tribunal rejected TikTok's challenge in 2024. Other companies designated as gatekeepers include Alphabet's Google, Meta Platforms, Apple, Amazon, Microsoft and Booking.com.

"The Court should dismiss the action brought by ByteDance (TikTok) against the decision of the Commission designating it as a gatekeeper under the Digital Markets Act," Advocate General Andrea Biondi said in his opinion. He endorsed the lower court's ruling. "The General Court did not make the errors of law alleged by ByteDance in rejecting those arguments. In particular, the fact that users also use other social networks does not, in itself, show that TikTok is not an important gateway," Biondi said. The judges, who are expected to rule in the coming months, follow such non-binding opinions in around four out of five cases. TikTok did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment. The DMA imposes a range of obligations on designated gatekeepers, with breaches potentially attracting fines of up to 10 per cent of a company's annual global turnover. Meta is also challenging the designation of gatekeeper for its Messenger and Marketplace services. The case is C-627/24 P Bytedance v Commission.

Oct 15 : Hyundai Motor America is recalling 94,622 vehicles in the US over a risk of fire while parked or driving due to the possibility of some front power seat motors overheating, the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said on Thursday. Here are some more details from NHTSA: • The front power seat motors may overheat due to a stuck power seat control switch, which can result in a fire while parked or driving • The affected vehicles include certain 2015-2016 Hyundai Genesis and 2017-2020 Genesis G80 models
